summary.text: Maynard’s prime-tuples theorem, combined with Chinese-remainder covering congruences and the admissible geometric shifts \(k!3^j\), yields arbitrarily long blocks of consecutive primes whose successive gaps strictly increase. The score rises by the length of each such block, contradicting the simultaneous existence of global lower and upper bounds.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
  P_0=2,0 P_1=3,0 P_2=5,0\ldots
\]
be the primes in increasing order, indexed from zero. For \(r\geq 1\), put
\[
  G_r=P_r-P_{r-1}.
\]
Thus \(G_r\) is the \(r\)-th prime gap in the indexing used by A092243. Define
\[
  \Delta_r=\operatorname{sgn}(G_r-G_{r-1})\in\{-1,0,1\}
  \qquad(r\geq2).
\]
The sequence in question is
\[
  A(n)=\sum_{r=2}^{n}\Delta_r
\]
for \(n\geq2\), with \(A(0)=A(1)=0\). In particular, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
  A(n+1)=A(n)+\Delta_{n+1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]

We shall prove that there are arbitrarily long strings of strictly increasing consecutive prime gaps. It will then follow from (1) that the score has arbitrarily large upward increments. Consequently the score cannot be bounded both below and above. Since the conjecture under consideration asserts, among its five clauses, both boundedness below and boundedness above, this disproves the conjunction.

The deep prime-distribution input is the following arithmetic-progression form of Maynard's prime-tuples theorem.

**Maynard prime-tuples theorem.** For every positive integer \(r\), there is an integer \(k\) with the following property. Let
\[
  h_0<h_1<\cdots<h_{k-1}
\]
be an admissible set of nonnegative shifts. Here admissible means that for every prime \(p\), the residues \(-h_0,\ldots,-h_{k-1}\pmod p\) do not exhaust all residue classes; equivalently, for every prime \(p\) there is a residue \(c_p\) such that
\[
  p\nmid c_p+h_i\qquad(0\leq i<k).
\]
If \(W>0\) and \(c\) satisfy
\[
  \gcd(W,c+h_i)=1\qquad(0\leq i<k),                              \tag{2}
\]
then, for every \(N\), there is an \(n\geq N\) for which at least \(r\) of
\[
  Wn+c+h_0,\ldots,Wn+c+h_{k-1}                                  \tag{3}
\]
are prime.

For completeness, the mathematical mechanism behind this form of the theorem is as follows. One first enlarges the fixed modulus \(W\), using admissibility and the Chinese remainder theorem, so that every sufficiently small prime divides the enlarged modulus while each selected residue \(c+h_i\) remains coprime to it. On the progression \(x\equiv c\pmod W\), one places nonnegative multidimensional Selberg weights
\[
 w(x)=\left(\sum_{d_i\mid x+h_i}\lambda_{d_0,\ldots,d_{k-1}}\right)^2,
\]
where the coefficients are supported on squarefree divisors composed of primes outside \(W\), with their product restricted to a suitable sieve level. Write
\[
 S_1=\sum_{x\leq X\atop x\equiv c\,({\rm mod}\,W)}w(x),
 \qquad
 S_2=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{x\leq X\atop x\equiv c\,({\rm mod}\,W)}
       w(x)\Lambda(x+h_i).
\]
Expansion of the square and counting simultaneous congruences give a quadratic form for \(S_1\). The corresponding expansion for \(S_2\), together with the positive-level distribution estimate for primes in arithmetic progressions (with a possible exceptional prime omitted from the sieve primes), gives a second quadratic form. The finite-dimensional Maynard choice of the coefficients makes the ratio of the latter main term to the former exceed any prescribed multiple of \(\log X\), provided \(k\) is chosen sufficiently large in terms of \(r\). All congruence-counting errors, the distribution errors, and the contribution from prime powers are smaller than the resulting positive margin when \(X\) is sufficiently large.

More explicitly, choosing the sieve dimension parameter large compared with \(r\) produces constants \(B>r\log(X+H)\), where \(H=\max h_i\), and weights for which
\[
 S_2>B S_1+E,                                                     \tag{4}
\]
where \(E\) dominates the total endpoint, progression-distribution, and nonprime prime-power errors. If every supported \(x\geq N\) had fewer than \(r\) prime values among \(x+h_i\), each such \(x\) would contribute at most \(r\log(X+H)w(x)\) from genuine primes. The terms with \(x<N\), and those for which \(\Lambda(x+h_i)\ne0\) although \(x+h_i\) is not prime, are bounded by the error allowance \(E\). Thus one would have
\[
 S_2\leq r\log(X+H)S_1+E,
\]
contradicting (4). Hence some supported \(x\geq N\) has at least \(r\) prime shifts. Because supported \(x\) lies in the prescribed progression, writing \(x=Wn+c\) gives (3). Taking \(X\) arbitrarily large gives arbitrarily large \(n\). This is the stated progression form of the Maynard theorem.

We next turn the Maynard theorem into a statement about *consecutive* primes. This requires a covering-congruence construction.

Fix any strictly increasing finite set of shifts
\[
  \mathcal H=\{h_0,\ldots,h_{k-1}\},
  \qquad H=h_{k-1}.
\]
Let
\[
  F=\{t:0\leq t\leq H,\ t\notin\mathcal H\}
\]
be the set of unselected positions in the interval \([0,H]\). For each \(t\in F\), choose a prime \(q_t\) so large that
\[
 q_t>H+t,                                                        \tag{5}
\]
and choose the \(q_t\)'s pairwise distinct. For example, one may take \(q_t\) to be the prime with index \(H+t+1\); these primes are distinct as \(t\) varies and are larger than \(H+t\).

By the Chinese remainder theorem there is an integer \(c\) satisfying
\[
  c\equiv -t\pmod {q_t}\qquad(t\in F).                          \tag{6}
\]
Let
\[
  W=\prod_{t\in F}q_t.
\]
(The empty-product case is harmless: then \(W=1\).) Equations (6) imply
\[
 q_t\mid c+t\quad(t\in F).                                      \tag{7}
\]
We claim that
\[
 \gcd(W,c+h_i)=1\quad\text{for every selected shift }h_i.        \tag{8}
\]
It is enough to show that no \(q_t\) divides \(c+h_i\). If one did, then (7) would give
\[
 h_i\equiv t\pmod {q_t}.
\]
But \(0\leq h_i,t\leq H<q_t\), by (5), so this congruence would force \(h_i=t\), contrary to \(t\in F\). This proves (8).

Furthermore, if \(n\) is sufficiently large, then every unselected number
\[
 Wn+c+t\qquad(t\in F)
\]
is composite. Indeed, \(q_t\mid W\) and \(q_t\mid c+t\), so \(q_t\mid Wn+c+t\). Once \(n>\max_{t\in F}q_t\), the number \(Wn+c+t\) is strictly larger than \(q_t\), and hence is not prime.

Now suppose \(\mathcal H\) is admissible. Apply the Maynard theorem, with the \(W,c\) just constructed and with \(n\) beyond the preceding threshold. It gives a translate
\[
 b=Wn+c
\]
for which at least \(r\) of the selected numbers \(b+h_i\) are prime. Every other integer in \([b,b+H]\) is of the form \(b+t\) with \(t\in F\), and is composite. Thus every prime in this entire interval occurs at a selected shift.

It follows that the first \(r\) primes at or after \(b\) all have the form \(b+h_i\). To spell out the indexing, let
\[
 \nu=\#\{p<b:p\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
Then \(P_\nu\) is the first prime at least \(b\), \(P_{\nu+1}\) the next one, and so forth. Since the interval contains at least \(r\) primes, \(P_\nu,\ldots,P_{\nu+r-1}\) all lie in \([b,b+H]\); and by the covering property, for every \(0\leq s<r\) there is an index \(j_s<k\) such that
\[
 P_{\nu+s}=b+h_{j_s}.                                            \tag{9}
\]
Since both the primes and the shifts are strictly increasing, the indices satisfy
\[
 j_0<j_1<\cdots<j_{r-1}.                                        \tag{10}
\]
We have therefore proved the following consequence: for every \(r\), a sufficiently large admissible set of shifts can be translated so that \(r\) consecutive primes occur at positions selected from that set.

We now choose a special admissible set whose successive selected differences grow very rapidly. Let \(k\) be the number supplied by the preceding result and put
\[
 h_j=k!\,3^j\qquad(0\leq j<k).                                  \tag{11}
\]
These shifts are strictly increasing. They are also admissible. Fix a prime \(p\).

* If \(p\leq k\), then \(p\mid k!\), and hence \(p\mid h_j\) for every \(j\). The residue \(c_p=1\) therefore avoids all the forbidden residues: \(p\nmid1+h_j\).

* If \(p>k\), there are at most \(k<p\) forbidden residue classes \(-h_j\pmod p\). They cannot exhaust the \(p\) residue classes modulo \(p\), so one can choose \(c_p\) outside them. Then again \(p\nmid c_p+h_j\) for every \(j\).

This covers all primes and proves admissibility.

The geometric shifts also have the key expanding-difference property. If
\[
 i_0<i_1<i_2,
\]
then
\[
 h_{i_1}-h_{i_0}<h_{i_2}-h_{i_1}.                               \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, \(h_{i_0}>0\), so
\[
 h_{i_1}-h_{i_0}<h_{i_1}.
\]
On the other hand, \(i_2\geq i_1+1\), and hence
\[
 h_{i_2}=k!3^{i_2}\geq3k!3^{i_1}=3h_{i_1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 h_{i_2}-h_{i_1}\geq2h_{i_1}>h_{i_1}-h_{i_0},
\]
which is (12).

Fix an arbitrary \(m\geq0\), and apply the consecutive-prime conclusion with \(r=m+2\) and with the geometric shifts (11). We obtain \(m+2\) consecutive primes
\[
 P_\nu,P_{\nu+1},\ldots,P_{\nu+m+1}

a satisfying (9), with
\[
 j_0<j_1<\cdots<j_{m+1}.
\]
For every \(0\leq s<m\), use (12) with \(i_0=j_s\), \(i_1=j_{s+1}\), and \(i_2=j_{s+2}\). Since the common translation \(b\) cancels, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_{\nu+s+1}-P_{\nu+s}
   &=h_{j_{s+1}}-h_{j_s}\\
   &<h_{j_{s+2}}-h_{j_{s+1}}\\
   &=P_{\nu+s+2}-P_{\nu+s+1}.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{13}
\]
In terms of prime gaps, (13) says
\[
 G_{\nu+s+1}<G_{\nu+s+2}\qquad(0\leq s<m).                    \tag{14}
\]
Because \(m\) was arbitrary, there are arbitrarily long runs of strictly increasing consecutive prime gaps.

It remains to translate this into the score. Suppose that for some \(n\geq1\),
\[
 G_n<G_{n+1}<\cdots<G_{n+m}.                                    \tag{15}
\]
Every one of the \(m\) comparisons in (15) has sign \(+1\). Repeatedly applying (1) gives
\[
 A(n+m)=A(n)+m.                                                   \tag{16}
\]
This can also be seen directly by splitting the defining cumulative sum at \(n\): all the added terms \(\Delta_{n+1},\ldots,\Delta_{n+m}\) equal \(1\).

Assume now, for contradiction, the two boundedness clauses of the proposed conjecture. Thus there are integers \(L,U\) such that
\[
 L\leq A(t)\leq U\qquad\text{for every }t.                      \tag{17}
\]
Necessarily \(L\leq U\) (for example, apply both inequalities to \(A(1)=0\)). Choose
\[
 m=U-L+1.
\]
By (14), there is an \(n\geq1\) for which (15) holds with this value of \(m\). Equations (16) and (17) then give
\[
 A(n+m)=A(n)+m
       \geq L+(U-L+1)
       =U+1.
\]
But the upper bound in (17), applied at \(n+m\), says \(A(n+m)\leq U\), a contradiction.

Therefore A092243 cannot be bounded both below and above. The stated conjecture is a single assertion comprising five affirmative clauses: existence of a later positive value, lower boundedness, upper boundedness, infinitely many positive values, and infinitely many negative values. Its lower- and upper-boundedness clauses are already mutually incompatible with the arbitrarily long increasing-gap runs proved above. Hence the full conjecture is false.
